analysis.one_liner: Taxes large employers the full value of the food, housing, and health benefits their employees need.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors eleven days before the session ended, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large companies a tax equal to 100% of the value of the federal benefits their employees receive — food stamps, school meals, Section 8 housing subsidies, and Medicaid. It would count part-time workers, contractors, and joint employees when deciding which companies are covered, and it would exempt companies that already pay everyone at least $15 an hour or hold under $100 million in assets. It would also make it illegal for a covered employer to ask job applicants whether they receive public benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large low-wage companies who currently rely on food stamps, Medicaid, school meals, or housing subsidies. The tax gives those employers a direct financial reason to raise pay above the exemption level so their workers no longer qualify for assistance — and the workers keep their benefits until that happens. Taxpayers also gain if employers absorb the cost of their workers' benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax on large employers equal to 100% of the SNAP, school meal, Section 8 housing, and Medicaid benefits their employees receive, shifting the cost of low wages back to the employer.
Exempts employers that pay all employees at least $15 an hour or hold under $100 million in assets, giving covered companies a clear path out of the tax by raising pay.
Counts part-time workers, independent contractors, and joint employees toward coverage, closing the main ways large employers keep headcount off their books.

Makes it an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to ask job applicants whether they receive federal benefits, enforced by the Labor Department with back pay and double damages for workers.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies with at least 500 full-time-equivalent employees that pay below $15 an hour and hold over $100 million in assets — big-box retailers, fast food chains, and warehouse operators whose workforces draw on public assistance. They would either pay a tax matching their employees' benefits dollar-for-dollar or raise wages above $15 an hour. Some of the cost could reach consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large low-wage retail and fast food employers

drawbacks.text: A tax tied to individual employees' household benefits is hard to administer: benefits like SNAP and Medicaid go to households, and the bill leaves the difficult matching job to Treasury regulations written in consultation with several agencies.

Covered employers could respond in ways that hurt workers, such as cutting hours, avoiding full-time status, shifting work to franchisees, or raising prices — and the bill does not stop employers from replacing lower-wage workers with automation.

The $15-an-hour exemption creates a cliff: a company just under the wage threshold faces a tax sized to its employees' benefits, which could pressure wages exactly up to the line without pushing higher.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a direct answer to a well-documented problem: taxpayers subsidize large, highly profitable companies whose full-time workers still need food and housing assistance. A dollar-for-dollar tax on those benefits, with a wage-based exit, is a sharper tool than most proposals of this kind. The real weaknesses are administrative — matching household benefits to individual employers will be complicated — and the risk that employers adjust through hours, prices, or automation rather than wages. On balance, a genuinely passed version would likely be a net gain for low-wage workers and taxpayers, but this bill never got far enough for those design questions to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final days of the session and referred to two committees, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on December 20, 2022, eleven days before the 117th Congress ended.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee, and neither committee took any action.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large low-wage employers are better off: because the bill never advanced, they face no tax on the public benefits their employees rely on, and the cost of those benefits stays with taxpayers. The bill's 11-day window and zero cosponsors meant it was unlikely to move regardless, so its death says as much about late-session timing as about organized opposition.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was his only action before the session ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Large low-wage employers (big-box retail, fast food, warehouse and logistics chains)
industries.note: These companies would owe a tax equal to the food, housing, and health benefits their employees receive, or raise every wage to $15 an hour to escape it. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the low-wage workers whose paychecks the bill targeted.

The bill counts independent contractors and joint employees toward employer size and benefit liability, which would reach staffing arrangements that currently shield client companies from benefit costs. Firms built on that model would face new exposure.
